findings.title: Not All Flips Are Conformity: Decomposing Stance Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
findings.authors: Xiqi Hao, Zengqing Wu, Yu-Xuan Qiu, Chuan Xiao, Ruiqi Xu, Shuyuan Zheng, Jianbin Qin
findings.why_relevant: The most dangerous construct-overlap paper found. It builds exactly the distinction our dual measure exists to make: it decomposes answer flips into spontaneous instability, stance-induced conformity, and reasoning-induced persuasion via controlled counterfactual conditions, arguing the raw flip rate conflates all three. Runs across three model families and GPQA-Diamond/MMLU-Pro, reports strict conformity at 29% and predominantly harmful (57-77% correct-to-wrong). Its information-gradient experiment injects vacuous reasoning and finds 20-39% error adoption among otherwise resistant agents - that is injected persuasive falsehood crossed with model-family variation. It also predicts harmful conformity from Round 0 features (AUC 0.79) and cuts it 13.6pp with targeted intervention. Its closing caveat - that reducing peer adoption does not improve accuracy because harmful and beneficial influence cannot be distinguished without correctness labels - is precisely the argument our truth-acquisition hazard is designed to answer, meaning a reviewer will ask why we are not simply extending this paper. Does not do capability matching, network topology, or hazard modeling; is debate, not multi-round network cascade. Found in the BACKWARD pass: the target cites it, and it is NOT in our known list.

findings.title: Belief Coevolution in a Social Network of Generalist and Specialist Large Language Models
findings.authors: Germans Savcisens, Samantha Dies, Courtney Maynard, Tina Eliassi-Rad
findings.why_relevant: The nearest structural neighbour to our entire design, and only ten days old. CoevolveSim studies belief diffusion in networked LLM populations where, in each round, an agent observes a summary of its neighbours' beliefs before updating - the same per-agent per-round belief measurement loop we specify. It manipulates network structure, social-role assignment, and domain specialization (generalist vs finetuned specialist) as controlled factors across 1,280 simulations. This occupies our multi-round networked-belief territory and a heterogeneity axis simultaneously. What it does NOT have is our core treatment: no injected falsehood, no adversarial seeded agents, no accuracy-matched diversity ladder separating architectural from stochastic and persona decorrelation, and no hazard/survival treatment. Its heterogeneity is specialist-vs-generalist finetuning, not cross-family architecture, and there is no evidence it matches populations on measured isolated accuracy. Strong Tier-A read: it is the paper whose framing we must differentiate against, and a likely baseline to cite. Eliassi-Rad is a senior network-science name, so this will be visible to reviewers.

findings.title: PlanFlip: Attacking Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Planning-Phase Prompt Injection
findings.authors: Yuhang Wang
findings.why_relevant: Hits threat #1 head-on and states our headline conclusion as an explicit claim: 'heterogeneous model diversity is a security prerequisite for multi-agent systems; redundancy within a homogeneous backbone provides no protection against planning-phase attacks.' Injects adversarial content (GoalSubstitution, PriorityInversion, ContextPollution, RoleConfusion), observes cascade amplification through downstream agents, and finds homogeneous pipelines create blind spots where Critic agents fail to detect corruption. Evaluated over 3,479 episodes across nine frontier LLMs. Also reports that stronger models are MORE vulnerable, which is a direct complication for our capability-matching rationale and worth engaging with explicitly. Crucially it does NOT control capability (it observes capability correlating with vulnerability rather than isolating it), does not separate architectural from persona/sampling diversity, and its domain is task-planning pipelines rather than belief propagation on a communication graph - the cascade is one injection fanning out to sub-tasks, not T rounds of peer-to-peer belief revision. Our differentiation is the capability-matched ladder and the belief-state hazard, not the diversity-helps direction.

findings.title: MESA: Prioritizing Vulnerable Communication Channels for Securing Multi-Agent Systems
findings.authors: Kunyang Li, Kyle Domico, Jonathan Gregory, Patrick McDaniel
findings.why_relevant: Crosses model-family heterogeneity with injected misinformation across network topologies - the same three-way intersection our design occupies - though for a different research question. Evaluates a dynamic misinformation attack pipeline across three MAS scenarios, EIGHT network topologies, and five open-source LLMs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma families. The paper treats diversity as a fixed backdrop rather than a treatment, does not match on capability, and studies workflow decision corruption rather than belief-state trajectories. Useful as a defensive-design citation and as a source of a real methodological warning.

findings.title: Emergence of Biased Consensus in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
findings.authors: Maya Okawa et al.
findings.why_relevant: THE most dangerous paper this channel found. It independently constructs almost exactly our diversity ladder's contrast set and runs it over multiple rounds. Verified from the HTML full text: heterogeneity is manipulated in THREE separate ways that map onto our D-levels — (i) different LLM backbones/families ('two distinct LLM backbones as agents, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4'; '11 commercial and open source LLMs spanning five major LLM families'), (ii) different sampling temperatures ('heterogeneous ensembles by mixing LLM agents with different sampling temperatures', T in {1.4,1.5,1.6}), and (iii) persona/prompt manipulation ('sycophancy level via prompting', 'persona-induced sycophancy') as a separate ablation. Multi-round: N=11 agents over 6 rounds synthetic, 6-10 agents over 7 rounds real-world, with per-round opinion trajectories plotted ('mean bias over seven rounds'). Topology: all-to-all plus sparse random interaction matrices with density parameter rho, P(J_ij=1)=rho — i.e. our complete/ER contrast. Population sizes 5-100, with a finite-size crossover. They fit a conformity parameter lambda_i inversely from trajectories. Headline claim: 'agent heterogeneity suppresses emergence by smoothing (rounding) this transition' — a diversity-as-defense result. WHAT SAVES US, and it must be stated plainly in our related work: (a) no injected falsehood — 'Because there are no correct answers in our tasks, any non-neutral consensus reflects bias', so this is EMERGENT bias, not an adversarially seeded plausible falsehood with a persuasive persona; (b) no capability matching — they mix Llama 3.1 405B/70B/8B 'without equalizing base accuracy', so their heterogeneity effect is confounded with capability, which is precisely the confound our matched design exists to remove; (c) no hazard/survival treatment and no truth-acquisition counterpart. Our novelty is now narrowed to: injected-falsehood adversary + capability-matched ladder + discrete-time capitulation hazard. The mere existence of architectural-vs-temperature separation over multi-round debate on a sparse graph is no longer novel.

findings.title: The Ringelmann Effect in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Scaling Law for Effective Team Size
findings.authors: Blaz Bertalanic, Carolina Fortuna
findings.why_relevant: Directly pre-empts our threat-4 claim on the accuracy axis. From the HTML full text: heterogeneous teams are 'equal-proportion mixes (Qwen2.5-7B / Llama-3.1-8B / Ministral-8B in 1:1:1 ratio)' at N in {3,6,9,15,30}, and the paper's stated conclusion is that 'only architectural diversity (heterogeneous teams) lowers c and escapes the hard-ceiling regime'. They use the word 'architectural diversity' for exactly the construct we do. Crucially they run a random-noise PLACEBO that isolates stochastic decorrelation from genuine peer content — 'peer answers drawn from a pre-generated pool of independent R1 outputs to other items, length-matched to debate' — and conclude that within homogeneous teams the apparent debate gain 'comes from re-evaluation, not peer content'. That placebo is a stronger stochastic-diversity control than our D1 temperature arm, and we should adopt or cite it. Multi-round: 'three communication rounds (R1 independent, R2-R3 post-debate)' with ablations k in {1,2,4,9,29} and tau in {1,...,6}, plus a mean-field theorem that k and tau enter only through the product k*tau — which, if true, materially constrains how we should reason about our T rounds crossed with graph degree. Sparse communication studied in Appendix I. WHAT SAVES US: no adversarial/injected misinformation anywhere; and explicitly NOT capability-matched — the HTML does not report solo-accuracy parity as a matching criterion, it only notes cross-family pairs agree less than within-family pairs. So their architectural-diversity effect is confounded with capability differences between Qwen/Llama/Ministral. Our matched design is the answer to this paper. Also no per-round belief state as a primary outcome (final round reported; per-round in appendices) and no hazard model.

findings.title: Collaborative QA using Interacting LLMs. Impact of Network Structure, Node Capability and Distributed Data
findings.authors: Adit Jain, Vikram Krishnamurthy, Yiming Zhang
findings.why_relevant: OFF-CHANNEL — this is NOT in the citing set and I could not confirm it cites 2508.17536; it surfaced via web search and I verified it via the arXiv API. Flagging it because it is structurally the closest thing to our formal model that I saw all session, and it collides with threats 2, 3 and 5 simultaneously. findings.title: Multi-Agent Teams Hold Experts Back
findings.authors: Aneesh Pappu, Batu El, Hancheng Cao, Carmelo di Nolfo, Yanchao Sun, Meng Cao, James Zou
findings.why_relevant: Hits threat 3 and, uniquely in this citing set, threat 1 in a weak form. The paper is built entirely around capability heterogeneity: self-organising LLM teams 'consistently fail to match their expert agent's performance, even when explicitly told who the expert is, incurring performance losses of up to 41.1%', and they decompose this into expert identification vs expert leveraging, finding leveraging is the bottleneck. That is a heterogeneity x adversary result and it points the OPPOSITE way to our hypothesis: it implies homogenising, consensus-seeking behaviour BUYS adversarial robustness at the cost of expertise use. If that generalises to our setting, our headline could invert. We should read the adversarial-agent section in full before finalising H1. WHAT SAVES US: the abstract does not establish that agents are matched on isolated accuracy (the point is precisely that they differ), the adversarial condition appears to be a secondary robustness check rather than a seeded-falsehood cascade, no communication graph is specified, and there is no hazard model.

findings.title: Breaking the Martingale Curse: Multi-Agent Debate via Asymmetric Cognitive Potential Energy (AceMAD)
findings.authors: not resolved (S2 record incomplete)
findings.why_relevant: The direct theoretical successor to our target and a must-cite: it names the target's result 'the Martingale Curse' and attacks it. Its stated diagnosis is our project's entire premise stated as someone else's motivation: 'This curse arises because correlated errors cause agents to converge toward erroneous consensus, where debate merely reinforces collective mistakes rather than filtering noise.' We claim architectural diversity decorrelates those errors; they instead break the martingale with a peer-prediction mechanism that creates 'submartingale drift toward truth' under nonlinear aggregation, proved via strictly proper scoring rules. This matters for our framing in two ways: (1) it establishes that error correlation is now the recognised bottleneck, so 'diversity decorrelates errors' is no longer a fresh observation and must be positioned as an empirical test of a known mechanism, not a discovery; (2) it gives a competing intervention (aggregation-side) against our competing intervention (population-composition-side), and a reviewer will ask which is cheaper. WHAT SAVES US: purely an aggregation/mechanism-design paper — no injected misinformation, no communication graph, no model-family manipulation, no capability matching, no hazard model. It operates on benchmark accuracy, not belief trajectories under attack.

channels.coverage_notes:
SCALE OF THE SCREEN. 109 papers screened in total: all 61 forward citations of arXiv:2508.17536 returned by the Semantic Scholar Graph API, plus all 48 entries in its reference list (backward pass). 19 are reported here at threat >= 2. The other 90 were screened out on full abstracts, not titles — the S2 payload returns complete abstracts, and I read them. The discard pile is dominated by inference-time-scaling and aggregation method papers (best-of-N, majority-voting variants, budget allocation, on-policy distillation, test-time orchestration), domain applications of debate (legal entailment, navigation, hateful memes, SciML, crypto package detection, corner-case curation, financial MAS surveys, clinical reviews), and evaluation/UQ surveys. None of these manipulate model-family composition against an injected falsehood.

COMPLETENESS OF THE FORWARD CHANNEL. The citation list is complete as far as Semantic Scholar knows: requesting offset=61 returned zero rows, so there is no unpaged tail. The newest citing paper is dated 2026-08-03, five days before today, so S2's index is current for this paper. Three caveats a human must close. (1) I could NOT cross-check against Google Scholar's "cited by" — it is not programmatically reachable from here and I did not attempt to defeat any bot-detection. S2 systematically under-counts non-arXiv venues (workshop papers, ACL/EMNLP Findings that never hit arXiv, and non-English venues), so the true citing set is a superset of these 61. (2) The OpenAlex cross-check FAILED — filter=cites:doi:10.48550/arXiv.2508.17536 returned an empty payload with no meta object, meaning the DOI did not resolve to an OpenAlex work ID. A human should resolve the OpenAlex work ID by title first, then re-run the cites filter; this is the single highest-value redo, because OpenAlex indexes venues S2 misses. (3) Connected Papers was not queried at all — no programmatic endpoint. Its co-citation neighbourhood would likely surface near-neighbours that cite the same ancestors without citing the target, which is exactly the blind spot of a pure forward search.

RATE LIMITING. The S2 API returned HTTP 429 partway through metadata enrichment. Consequence: authors and exact venues are unresolved for 8 of the 19 findings (marked "not resolved" in the authors field). Titles and arXiv IDs are correct and every identifier resolves; only the author strings are missing. A human with an S2 API key can fill these in one batched call. Two identifiers in the citing set had no arXiv ID at all and could not be chased: "Tackling Model Bias via Game-theoretic Multi-agent Collaboration Framework for Hateful Meme Classification" (CorpusId 289925133, no abstract, no year — screened out on title as image-classification work) and two journal entries (Knowledge-Based Systems, IP&M) that are domain benchmarks.

VERIFICATION STANDARD USED. Findings split into two tiers and the distinction matters for the bib. Tier 1, abstract PAGE fetched and in several cases the HTML full text read, so method claims are quotable: 2608.02827, 2606.02646, 2511.07784, 2602.01011, 2512.03097.
